file.content:
# Instance file format

Each file in `data/` is a JSON object describing one unit commitment instance.
Power is in MW, time in hourly periods, and costs in dollars.

## Top level

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `time_periods` | Number of periods in the planning horizon, T |
| `demand` | Array of length T: system load in each period |
| `reserves` | Array of length T: spinning reserve requirement in each period |
| `thermal_generators` | Object mapping each generator's name to its data |
| `renewable_generators` | Object mapping each renewable generator's name to its data |

The instances have no transmission network.

## Each thermal generator

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | The generator's name |
| `must_run` | 1 if the generator must be on in every period, otherwise 0 |
| `power_output_minimum`, `power_output_maximum` | Minimum and maximum output when on |
| `ramp_up_limit`, `ramp_down_limit` | Ramp-up and ramp-down rates, per period |
| `ramp_startup_limit`, `ramp_shutdown_limit` | Start-up and shut-down rates |
| `time_up_minimum`, `time_down_minimum` | Minimum up time and minimum down time, in periods |
| `unit_on_t0` | 1 if the generator is on in period 0, otherwise 0 |
| `power_output_t0` | Output in period 0 |
| `time_up_t0`, `time_down_t0` | Number of periods the generator has been on, or off, as of period 0 |
| `startup` | Array of `{lag, cost}`, ordered by increasing `lag`: the start-up cost `cost` applies when the generator has been off for at least `lag` periods |
| `piecewise_production` | Array of `{mw, cost}`, ordered by increasing `mw`: the points of the piecewise linear production cost curve, where `cost` is the hourly cost of producing `mw` |

## Each renewable generator

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | The generator's name |
| `power_output_minimum`, `power_output_maximum` | Arrays of length T: minimum and maximum output in each period |

pdftotext -layout paper.pdf /tmp/paper.txt; wc -l /tmp/paper.txt; pdfinfo paper.pdf | grep Pages; head -c 1800 data/rts_gmlc_2020-01-27.json; echo; python3 -I - <<'EOF'
import json,glob,collections
for f in sorted(glob.glob('data/*.json')):
    d=json.load(open(f))
    print(f, list(d.keys()), 'T',d['time_periods'],'G',len(d['thermal_generators']),'R',len(d['renewable_generators']))
    tg=d['thermal_generators']
    g0=next(iter(tg.values()))
    print(' keys',sorted(g0.keys()))
    print(' dem',min(d['demand']),max(d['demand']),' res',min(d['reserves']),max(d['reserves']))
    stats=collections.Counter()
    for n,g in tg.items():
        Pm,PM=g['power_output_minimum'],g['power_output_maximum']
        SU,SD,RU,RD=g['ramp_startup_limit'],g['ramp_shutdown_limit'],g['ramp_up_limit'],g['ramp_down_limit']
        UT,DT=g['time_up_minimum'],g['time_down_minimum']
        if n!=g['name']: stats['name_mismatch']+=1
        if g['must_run']: stats['must_run']+=1
        if UT==1: stats['UT1']+=1
        if UT==0: stats['UT0']+=1
        if DT==0: stats['DT0']+=1
        if DT==1: stats['DT1']+=1
        if SU<Pm: stats['SU<Pmin']+=1
        if SD<Pm: stats['SD<Pmin']+=1
        if SU>PM: stats['SU>Pmax']+=1
        if SD>PM: stats['SD>Pmax']+=1
        if SU!=SD: stats['SU!=SD']+=1
        if RU<=0 or RD<=0: stats['ramp0']+=1
        if RU>PM-Pm: stats['RU_nonbinding']+=1
        if Pm==PM: stats['Pmin=Pmax']+=1
        if Pm==0: stats['Pmin=0']+=1
        pw=g['piecewise_production']
        if abs(pw[0]['mw']-Pm)>1e-9: stats['pw0!=Pmin']+=1
        if abs(pw[-1]['mw']-PM)>1e-9: stats['pwlast!=Pmax']+=1
        if len(pw)<2: stats['pw<2']+=1
        sl=[(pw[i+1]['cost']-pw[i]['cost'])/(pw[i+1]['mw']-pw[i]['mw']) if pw[i+1]['mw']>pw[i]['mw'] else None for i in range(len(pw)-1)]
        if None in sl: stats['pw_dup_mw']+=1
        elif any(sl[i+1]<sl[i]-1e-9 for i in range(len(sl)-1)): stats['nonconvex']+=1
        su=g['startup']
        if su[0]['lag']!=DT: stats['lag0!=DT']+=1
        stats['startcats=%d'%len(su)]+=1
        if any(su[i+1]['cost']<su[i]['cost'] for i in range(len(su)-1)): stats['su_decreasing']+=1
        if any(su[i+1]['lag']<=su[i]['lag'] for i in range(len(su)-1)): stats['su_lag_nonincr']+=1
        on=g['unit_on_t0']
        if on and g['power_output_t0']<=0: stats['on_p0=0']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']<Pm: stats['on_p0<Pmin']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']>PM: stats['on_p0>Pmax']+=1
        if not on and g['power_output_t0']!=0: stats['off_p0!=0']+=1
        if on and g['time_up_t0']<=0: stats['on_tup0=0']+=1
        if on and g['time_down_t0']!=0: stats['on_tdn!=0']+=1
        if not on and g['time_down_t0']<=0: stats['off_tdn0=0']+=1
        if not on and g['time_up_t0']!=0: stats['off_tup!=0']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']>SD and g['time_up_t0']>=UT and False: pass
        if Pm>SU: stats['Pm>SU']+=1
        for k in g:
            if k not in ('name','startup','piecewise_production') and not isinstance(g[k],(int,float)): stats['type_'+k]+=1
    print(' ',dict(stats))
    rn=d['renewable_generators']
    rm=[sum(r['power_output_minimum'][t] for r in rn.values()) for t in range(d['time_periods'])]
    rM=[sum(r['power_output_maximum'][t] for r in rn.values()) for t in range(d['time_periods'])]
    print(' ren min',max(rm) if rm else None,' max',max(rM) if rM else None)
EOF

    print('  demand-renmin min',min(d['demand'][t]-rm[t] for t in range(T)))

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: computer-use
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: chrome-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: built-in-browser
commands.description: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:deep-research
commands.description: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. commands.name: import-memory

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Solves each instance's LP relaxation and MIP in turn, 600 s limit per solve.
# Outputs go to results/<instance>.{lp,mip}.txt, .log, and .mip.csv.
# With an argument, also passes it as --variant and tags the file names with it.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
mkdir -p results
variant="${1:-}"
tag=""
extra=()
if [ -n "$variant" ]; then
    tag=".$variant"
    extra=(--variant "$variant")
fi
for f in data/*.json; do
    name="$(basename "$f" .json)"
    build/uc_solve --relax --time-limit 600 "${extra[@]}" --log "results/$name$tag.lp.log" \
        "$f" > "results/$name$tag.lp.txt" 2>&1
    build/uc_solve --time-limit 600 "${extra[@]}" --log "results/$name$tag.mip.log" \
        --solution "results/$name$tag.mip.csv" "$f" > "results/$name$tag.mip.txt" 2>&1
done

- DATA_FORMAT.md: instance format.
- src/model.c, src/model.h: the model builder. This is the main thing to review.
- src/instance.c, src/instance.h: data loading and preprocessing into the paper's notation.
- src/main.c: CLI and CSV output.

Setting: single-bus instances (no network), so (64) is dropped. C_LP=10000, C_RP=1000, C^w=0. The defaults in model_default_options are the model that counts. The variants in model_apply_variant are diagnostics, so you need not review the base model closely.

3. Off-time arcs x(t',t): which arcs exist, including those from a shut-down before the horizon, and whether each gets the right start-up category and objective coefficient. A start-up cost with lag L applies when the unit has been off at least L periods. Use time_down_t0 to work out the actual off duration by hand for a small example.
4. C^R, C^l and the curve preprocessing, the start-up category preprocessing, T^RU, T^RD, U and D in instance.c.

The code departs from the printed paper in a few places, on purpose. Do not assume that either the paper or the code is right where they differ. For each difference, derive the correct version yourself: take a small concrete generator and test whether a physically feasible schedule is cut off, or an infeasible one allowed. Report which version is valid.

Report only real defects or real doubts, each with file:line, the equation, a concrete example of what goes wrong, and your confidence. List separately each place where the code and the printed paper differ, with your verdict on which is valid and why. If an equation is correct, one short line saying so is enough. Keep the report under 600 words.

1	# Instance file format
2	
3	Each file in `data/` is a JSON object describing one unit commitment instance.
4	Power is in MW, time in hourly periods, and costs in dollars.
5	
6	## Top level
7	
8	| Field | Meaning |
9	|---|---|
10	| `time_periods` | Number of periods in the planning horizon, T |
11	| `demand` | Array of length T: system load in each period |
12	| `reserves` | Array of length T: spinning reserve requirement in each period |
13	| `thermal_generators` | Object mapping each generator's name to its data |
14	| `renewable_generators` | Object mapping each renewable generator's name to its data |
15	
16	The instances have no transmission network.
17	
18	## Each thermal generator
19	
20	| Field | Meaning |
21	|---|---|
22	| `name` | The generator's name |
23	| `must_run` | 1 if the generator must be on in every period, otherwise 0 |
24	| `power_output_minimum`, `power_output_maximum` | Minimum and maximum output when on |
25	| `ramp_up_limit`, `ramp_down_limit` | Ramp-up and ramp-down rates, per period |
26	| `ramp_startup_limit`, `ramp_shutdown_limit` | Start-up and shut-down rates |
27	| `time_up_minimum`, `time_down_minimum` | Minimum up time and minimum down time, in periods |
28	| `unit_on_t0` | 1 if the generator is on in period 0, otherwise 0 |
29	| `power_output_t0` | Output in period 0 |
30	| `time_up_t0`, `time_down_t0` | Number of periods the generator has been on, or off, as of period 0 |
31	| `startup` | Array of `{lag, cost}`, ordered by increasing `lag`: the start-up cost `cost` applies when the generator has been off for at least `lag` periods |
32	| `piecewise_production` | Array of `{mw, cost}`, ordered by increasing `mw`: the points of the piecewise linear production cost curve, where `cost` is the hourly cost of producing `mw` |
33	
34	## Each renewable generator
35	
36	| Field | Meaning |
37	|---|---|
38	| `name` | The generator's name |
39	| `power_output_minimum`, `power_output_maximum` | Arrays of length T: minimum and maximum output in each period |

**Verdict: I found no definite defects in the default model.** I checked it by reading and hand derivation only; nothing was run. I did not read NOTES.md, so these verdicts are independent of it. Three doubts remain, and five places differ from the printed paper.

**Doubts**

1. **model.c:522-529, (67), medium confidence.** The reserve row adds `pw` but not `s+ - s-`.
   - Headroom is really Σp̄ + pW + s+ − s− − D, so the argument for adding `pw` also applies to the slacks.
   - Example: D=100, capacity 90, R=0. Then s+=10 also forces sR=10, adding $10,000/h for a shortfall that isn't real.
   - It only matters when the slacks are nonzero. The printed row has the same gap.
2. **model.c:105, instance.c:368, (38)/(40), high on the logic, impact depends on the data.** Historical v is correct only if p(0) matches it.
   - Example: Pmax=100, SU=50, RU=RD=10, UT=4, up0=1, p0=100.
   - (38) at t=1 gives p̄(1)≤60, while (36) gives p(1)≥90, so the whole model is infeasible.
   - instance.c:342 warns about this.
3. **model.c:474-475, (3b), high on the logic.** With must_run=1, on0=0, down0=1, DT=4, the code sets lb=1 and ub=0, which is infeasible. instance.c:336 warns, but I did not check whether the data contains such a unit.

Decreasing start-up costs also break (61), because arcs with a positive coefficient stay at 0. The paper assumes non-decreasing costs, and the code warns.

**Differences from the printed paper**

| Item | Verdict | Test |
|---|---|---|
| (4)/(5) start at min(UT,T), model.c:115-119 | Code valid | UT=30, T=24: printed has no rows, so start t=1, stop t=5 is allowed. The code's row at T blocks it and cuts nothing feasible. |
| (41) K^SU self-reference read as K^SD, model.c:209 | Code valid | v(t−K^SU) and w(t+1+K^SD) span UT−1 periods, so they are exclusive. It reduces to (39), as the text requires. |
| (41) tail operands, model.c:222 | Code valid, printed invalid | See example A. Supplement (88a) has the code's order. |
| (41) tail K^SD instead of T^RD, model.c:222 | Code valid | See example B. |
| (48) [·]+ operands, model.c:285-286 | Code valid, printed invalid | See example C. The code's order matches (23). |
| (67) renewable term, model.c:527 | Code valid | D=100, R=10, Pmax=100, wind 50: p=50 leaves 50 headroom, yet printed charges sR=10. With zero slacks, the code equals (68). |

- **Example A:** Pmin=0, Pmax=100, SD=50, RD=30, SU=40, RU=45, UT=3, so K^SD=1 and K^SU=0. The run p=40, 80, 50 is feasible. The printed coefficient [85−80]+=5 gives p(t)≤75, which cuts it off. The code's [80−85]+=0 gives p(t)≤80.
- **Example B:** SU=SD=RU=RD=10, Pmax=100, UT=3, so K^SD=2 and K^SU=−1. With T^RD, the run p=10, 20, 10 gets RHS 100−70−90=−60, which is infeasible. The code gives 10, which is exact.
- **Example C:** Pmin=10, P̄^l={10,30,50}, SU=20, SD=40, UT=1, one-period run. For l=2, printed (48a) gives p²≤20−20−10=−10, so the run is infeasible. The code gives 0 for l=2 and 10 for l=1, so p≤20, which is exact.

The tail cases the paper does not discuss, K^SU=−1 and τ=0, are also valid. The coefficient is at most P̄−a, where a=SU+(K^SU+1)RU, and with both terms active the row gives exactly min(a, SD+K^SD·RD).

**Preprocessing departures, all valid**
- SU and SD are clipped to P̄, which keeps T^RU, T^RD and the coefficients nonnegative.
- UT and DT are floored at 1.
- Categories are remapped with T¹=DT.
- The cost curve is restricted to [P_, P̄].
- must_run becomes a lower bound on u.

**Equations that are correct**
- **(2), (3):** correct, including u(0), U and D.
- **(4), (5):** correct. Historical terms appear only in the clamped row at T, and they are consistent with (3).
- **(17), (23a/b), (38), (40):** correct, including the condition on (40). Historical v only reaches t≤U, where u is forced on. For a unit off at t=0, historical v of 0 is safe.
- **(41):** correct, and the left side is p′. Every pair of active v and w terms is excluded by UT, except the tail pair, which is handled by the operands above.
- **(35), (36):** correct, including the t=1 right-hand sides and p′(0).
- **(43), (44), (46), (48), C^v, C^w:** correct.
- **(59), (60), (61):** correct.
- **(62), (65), (66), (69):** correct.
- **T^RU, T^RD, C^R, C^l:** correct, checked with a hand example where the curve extends beyond [P_, P̄].

**Off-time arcs, correct**
- **Hand check:** take down0=3, DT=2, lags {1,4,10}, which become {2,4,10}. The shut-down is at t′=−2.
  - Start at t=1 means 3 periods off, which is the hottest category.
  - Start at t=2 means 4 periods off, which is the next category.
  - Start at t=8 means 10 periods off, so there is no arc and the cold cost applies.
- **False arcs:** an arc that spans an intervening run is permitted, as in the paper, but it never pays when costs are non-decreasing.

**Not reviewed:** the variants and the base model, as you said. In json.c I only confirmed that booleans load as 0 or 1. main.c's CSV output looks correct.

| (41) tail K^SD instead of T^RD, model.c:222 | Code valid | See example B. |
| (48) [·]+ operands, model.c:285-286 | Code valid, printed invalid | See example C. The code's order matches (23). |
| (67) renewable term, model.c:527 | Code valid | D=100, R=10, Pmax=100, wind 50: p=50 leaves 50 headroom, yet printed charges sR=10. With zero slacks, the code equals (68). |

- **Example A:** Pmin=0, Pmax=100, SD=50, RD=30, SU=40, RU=45, UT=3, so K^SD=1 and K^SU=0. The run p=40, 80, 50 is feasible. The printed coefficient [85−80]+=5 gives p(t)≤75, which cuts it off. The code's [80−85]+=0 gives p(t)≤80.
- **Example B:** SU=SD=RU=RD=10, Pmax=100, UT=3, so K^SD=2 and K^SU=−1. With T^RD, the run p=10, 20, 10 gets RHS 100−70−90=−60, which is infeasible. The code gives 10, which is exact.
- **Example C:** Pmin=10, P̄^l={10,30,50}, SU=20, SD=40, UT=1, one-period run. For l=2, printed (48a) gives p²≤20−20−10=−10, so the run is infeasible. The code gives 0 for l=2 and 10 for l=1, so p≤20, which is exact.

The tail cases the paper does not discuss, K^SU=−1 and τ=0, are also valid. The coefficient is at most P̄−a, where a=SU+(K^SU+1)RU, and with both terms active the row gives exactly min(a, SD+K^SD·RD).

**Preprocessing departures, all valid**
- SU and SD are clipped to P̄, which keeps T^RU, T^RD and the coefficients nonnegative.
- UT and DT are floored at 1.
- Categories are remapped with T¹=DT.
- The cost curve is restricted to [P_, P̄].
- must_run becomes a lower bound on u.

**Equations that are correct**
- **(2), (3):** correct, including u(0), U and D.
- **(4), (5):** correct. Historical terms appear only in the clamped row at T, and they are consistent with (3).
- **(17), (23a/b), (38), (40):** correct, including the condition on (40). Historical v only reaches t≤U, where u is forced on. For a unit off at t=0, historical v of 0 is safe.
- **(41):** correct, and the left side is p′. Every pair of active v and w terms is excluded by UT, except the tail pair, which is handled by the operands above.
- **(35), (36):** correct, including the t=1 right-hand sides and p′(0).
- **(43), (44), (46), (48), C^v, C^w:** correct.
- **(59), (60), (61):** correct.
- **(62), (65), (66), (69):** correct.
- **T^RU, T^RD, C^R, C^l:** correct, checked with a hand example where the curve extends beyond [P_, P̄].

**Off-time arcs, correct**
- **Hand check:** take down0=3, DT=2, lags {1,4,10}, which become {2,4,10}. The shut-down is at t′=−2.
  - Start at t=1 means 3 periods off, which is the hottest category.
  - Start at t=2 means 4 periods off, which is the next category.
  - Start at t=8 means 10 periods off, so there is no arc and the cold cost applies.
- **False arcs:** an arc that spans an intervening run is permitted, as in the paper, but it never pays when costs are non-decreasing.

input.content:
# Results: formulation T on the seven instances

All seven MIPs reached the 0.01% gap well inside the 600 s limit, and all seven LP relaxations solved to optimality.

The model departs from the paper's printed text in a few places. One of them, the renewable term in the reserve row (67), changes the objective by up to 135%. See [Effect of the reserve equation](#effect-of-the-reserve-equation) and `NOTES.md`.

| `rts_gmlc_2020-12-23` | 80719.254 | 86297.500 | 39137 | 21425 | 44488 | 206976 |

| `rts_gmlc_2020-07-06` | 3729194.920899 | 3728825.770989 | 3729194.920899 | 3728823.125816 | yes |
| `rts_gmlc_2020-12-23` | 2707509.117416 | 2707260.274187 | 2707458.250828 | 2707196.479605 | yes |
| `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3` | 48409.123688 | 48404.470950 | 48407.906437 | 48404.148645 | yes |
| `ca_Scenario400_reserves_1` | 33590.742186 | 33587.387286 | 33590.159078 | 33587.075872 | yes |
| `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` | 41483157.102869 | 41482399.553225 | 41483616.907983 | 41482325.156730 | yes |
| `ferc_2015-04-01_lw` | 57001082.949048 | 56999603.005677 | 57004338.160063 | 56999545.483832 | yes |

Equation numbers refer to the paper, and "supplement" to the online supplement bound into `paper.pdf`. The code is in `src/model.c` (the formulation), `src/instance.c` (data), `src/json.c` (the reader) and `src/main.c` (the command line).

The LP effects below were measured with `--variant`, on the instances named in each entry.

## Departures from the printed paper

### 1. Reserve constraint (67): renewable output added. This changes results substantially.

- **Printed:** `sum p̄(t) + s_R(t) >= D(t) + R(t)`.
- **Implemented:** `sum p̄(t) + p_W(t) + s_R(t) >= D(t) + R(t)`.

**Reason.**
- Section 3.9.3 presents (67) and (68) as two ways to write one requirement, chosen by which reserve variable is in use, and states that `r = p̄ - p`.
- Substituting that into (68) and using the balance (65) gives `sum p̄ + p_W + s + s_R >= D + R`. So the printed form matches (68) only when there are no renewables. The paper takes (67) from Carrion and Arroyo (2006) and Ostrowski et al. (2012).
- As printed, thermal capacity alone must cover the whole load, however much renewable energy is being used. On `rts_gmlc_2020-01-27` the model then curtails 61% of zero-cost renewable energy, against 14% otherwise, to keep thermal units on.

**Effect.** The MIP objective rises by 135%, 27%, 27%, 77%, 71% and 0.7% on the six instances with renewables. `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3` has none and is unaffected. Full figures are in `RESULTS.md`.

**Supporting evidence, which is only suggestive.** The paper gives T times of 88.8, 19.4 and 6.8 s on the RTS days January, December and July. The default model takes 40.75, 8.79 and 4.46 s, the same order. The printed form takes 5.11, 6.67 and 118.32 s, the reverse order. The solver version and machine differ from the paper's.

**This is the one decision you may want to overrule.** It departs from an equation that is well defined as printed, on the ground that the printed form is inconsistent with the paper's own statements. `--variant reserve-printed` gives the literal form.

I added only `p_W`, not the load slacks `s+ - s-`, as the smallest change. The exact equivalent of (68) would include them. The two forms differ only when a slack is nonzero, and every slack was zero in all seven MIP and LP solutions.

### 2. Rows (4) and (5) when UT or DT exceeds T

- **Printed:** `t ∈ {UT,…,T}` and `t ∈ {DT,…,T}`.
- **Implemented:** `t ∈ {min(UT,T),…,T}` and `t ∈ {min(DT,T),…,T}`, with sums clipped to the horizon and any historical `v` or `w` moved to the right side. This is identical to the printed form when UT, DT ≤ T.

**Reason.** The FERC data has up to UT=168 and DT=168 on a 48-period horizon: 41 and 102 such units in `ferc_2015-01-01_hw`, 39 and 100 in `ferc_2015-04-01_lw`. The printed range is empty for them, so nothing enforces their minimum times. The single row at t=T restores it: a start at any period forces the unit on at T, and allows no second start.

**Effect.** With the rows exactly as printed (`--variant updown-printed`), `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` falls from 41483157 to 36221169 (−12.7%), and its LP from 41480391 to 36213647. With the clamp, the LP equals that of rows in all periods (`--variant updown-all-periods`) on the three instances tested: `rts_gmlc_2020-07-06`, `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3`, `ferc_2015-01-01_hw`.

I did not add rows for t < UT in general, since the printed set is correct for integer solutions and adding them left those LP values unchanged. A spurious pair `v(t)=w(t)=1` with t below UT or DT is excluded by the rows at t=UT and t=DT.

### 3. K^SU in (41): typo corrected

- **Printed:** `K^SU(t) = min{T^RU, UT-2-[K^SU(t)]^+, t-1}`, which defines K^SU in terms of itself.
- **Implemented:** `[K^SD(t)]^+` in place of `[K^SU(t)]^+`.

**Reason.** A `v(t-i)` and a `w(t+1+j)` in the same row must not both be 1. That needs `i+j+1 < UT`, so the largest i is `UT-2-K^SD`. With this reading, (41) reduces to (39) when UT ≥ T^RU+T^RD+2, as the text says it should.

### 4. Extra term of (41): operands reversed and T^RD replaced

- **Printed:** `-[(SU+(K^SU+1)RU) - (SD+T^RD RD)]^+ v(t-(K^SU+1))`.
- **Implemented:** `-[(SD+K^SD RD) - (SU+(K^SU+1)RU)]^+ v(t-(K^SU+1))`.

**Reason for the operand order.** The printed order cuts off feasible schedules. For example, take P_=0, P̄=100, SU=40, RU=45, SD=50, RD=30, UT=3. The run 40, 80, 50 is feasible, but the printed term gives `p <= 75` at the middle period. The text calls this term "similar to (23b)", and (23b) has the reverse order. So does the supplement's (88a).

**Reason for K^SD.** (88a) only covers `K^SD = T^RD`. When `K^SD < T^RD`, both the tail `v` and `w(t+1+K^SD)` can equal 1, and using T^RD makes the right side too small. For example, SU=SD=RU=RD=10, P̄=100, UT=3 at a period where `K^SD=2`, `K^SU=-1`: the run 10, 20, 10 gets a right side of −60. With K^SD the right side is exactly `min(a, SD+K^SD RD)`.

**Effect.** None measured on the LP. The printed coefficient is zero on every row of `rts_gmlc_2020-07-06` and `ferc_2015-01-01_hw`, so on those two the printed form equals having no term. The implemented coefficient adds 4065 nonzeros on `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` and none on `rts_gmlc_2020-07-06` or `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3`, and leaves the LP objective unchanged on all three.

### 5. Equation (48): operands of [·]^+ reversed

- **Printed:** (48a) has `[C^v-C^w]^+ w(t+1)` and (48b) has `[C^w-C^v]^+ v(t)`.
- **Implemented:** (48a) has `[C^w-C^v]^+ w(t+1)` and (48b) has `[C^v-C^w]^+ v(t)`.

**Reason.** The text says (48) follows (23). In (23a) the `w` coefficient is `[SU-SD]^+`, and `SU-SD` equals `C^w-C^v` on a segment both limits fall inside, so the printed order is the opposite of (23). It is also invalid. With P_=10, breakpoints 10, 30, 50, SU=20, SD=40, UT=1, printed (48a) gives `p^2 <= -10` for a one-period run, which makes that feasible run infeasible.

**Effect.** LP objective unchanged on `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` and `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3`. MIP effect not measured. Both forms coincide whenever SU=SD.

### 6. SU and SD clipped to P̄

**Implemented.** `SU = min(SU, P̄)` and `SD = min(SD, P̄)`.

**Reason.** 574 of the 610 units in each CAISO instance have limits above P̄, such as SU=61.725 with P̄=5.75. Then `P̄-SU` is negative, which turns the reductions in (23) and (38) into increases and allows `p̄ > P̄`. A limit above P̄ never binds, so clipping removes no feasible schedule. The paper assumes `P̄-SU >= 0` throughout, in its definition of T^RU for instance. I did not measure the effect on the LP.

## Where the paper leaves something open

| Topic | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `must_run` | `u(t) >= 1` for all t | Only the data format defines it; the paper mentions must-run units only in the instance description. |
| U and D in (3) | `U = max(UT - time_up_t0, 0)` if on at period 0, `D = max(DT - time_down_t0, 0)` if off | The nomenclature defines them only as the hours required on or off. |
| (3) | Implemented as bounds on u | Equivalent, and the paper expects presolve to remove these variables. |
| Historical `v` | `v(1-time_up_t0) = 1` for a unit on at period 0; otherwise 0 | Section 3 says to use historical data. Earlier starts cannot enter a row. `p(0)` is consistent with this on all seven instances, and LP objective on `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` is the same without it. |
| Historical `w` | `w(1-time_down_t0) = 1` for a unit off at period 0; otherwise 0 | Same reason. It is the only shut-down before the horizon that can pair with a start-up in it. |
| Off-time arcs | `x(t',t)` for `DT <= t-t' <= TC-1`, for `t'` in the horizon or at the historical shut-down. (60) at that shut-down has right side 1. | The nomenclature includes times before the horizon. An off time of n periods at period 0 and a start at t gives an off duration of `t+n-1`, matching "off for at least `lag` periods". |
| Rows at `t = T` | `w(T+1) = 0` in (23), (38), (46), (48) | Section 3 sets `v` and `w` beyond the horizon to 0, so no shut-down limit applies at T. |
| `(38)` and `(40)` for `UT = 1` | Included, with the sum empty or one term | Table 3 has no condition. These rows are dominated by (23) but harmless. |
| `(23)` for `UT > 1` | Not used | The paper defines it for G^1 only. (38) generalizes (20) for the others. |
| Left side of (41) | `p'`, not `p̄'` | It is printed with `p`, and its ramp-down terms do not limit available power. |
| `K^SD(t) <= 0` | (41) omitted | The paper says so. |
| `p'(0)` | `p(0) - P_` if on, else 0 | From (12). |
| Variables | `p`, `p̄`, `c^p`, `c^SU`, `c^SD`, and `s` are not created | (12), (13), (44), (61), (62) and (66) substitute them out, as the paper does for cost variables. `s` is `s+ - s-`. |
| Renewables | One aggregate variable per period, bounds the sum of the unit bounds | (63), for one bus. Only the total is reported. |
| Network | (64) dropped; flow sums in (65) empty | Section 3.9.2, for one bus. |
| `T^RU`, `T^RD` | Floor computed with an added 1e-9 | Protects against rounding in ratios that are exact in the data. |
| Solver settings | Gurobi defaults, 16 threads, except `MIPGap` and `TimeLimit` | Matches the paper's Section 6.3, which keeps defaults apart from the limit and gap. |

## Data preprocessing that is present but not used here

`uc_solve` prints a `data warning` to stderr whenever one of these applies. On the seven instances the only warnings are SU and SD above P̄ (CAISO) and UT and DT above T (FERC), so none of the following is used.

- **Start-up categories:** the paper sets `T^1 = DT`. A first lag above DT is extended down to DT, and categories wholly below DT are dropped.
- **Cost curves:** restricted to `[P_, P̄]` by interpolation, with repeated points removed, so that `P̄^l > P_` and `P̄^0 = P_`. `C^R` is the curve's cost at `P_`.
- **UT, DT below 1:** set to 1.
- **Not repaired, warned only:** decreasing start-up costs, which would break (61); non-convex curves; `p(0)` above `SU + (time_up_t0-1) RU`, which would make the historical `v` terms infeasible; and a must-run unit required to stay off, which is infeasible.

## Output choices the task left open

- `--relax --solution`: `on` is `u` rounded at 0.5, as the format requires 0 or 1. `power` and `available` use the fractional `u`.
- In a MIP solution, `u` is rounded before computing `power` and `available`, which removes integrality noise.
- Besides `objective=` and `bound=`, stdout has `gap=`, `nodes=`, `status=`, `runtime=`, `size=` and totals for slacks and renewables. The Gurobi log is not sent to the console.
- If there is no solution, it prints `objective=nan` and exits 1. An LP stopped by the limit counts as no solution, since its point is not the relaxation's value. A MIP with no finite bound yet prints `bound=-inf`.
- Generator names containing commas or quotes are quoted in the CSV. None of the seven instances has one.

## Options beyond the specified command line

- `--log FILE` keeps the Gurobi log.
- `--variant NAME` selects a diagnostic departure from the default model, and may be repeated. The names are `reserve-printed`, `updown-printed`, `updown-all-periods`, `tail-none`, `tail-printed`, `pw48-printed`, `no-hist-v` and `base`, along with names that restate the defaults. They exist only to measure the decisions above.

## Verification

**What was run.** The checks reported in `RESULTS.md`: T against the `base` model on all seven instances, hand checks of one period and one unit, an independent read-through of the code against the paper, and tests of the early-stop and bad-input paths.

**What could not be run.** This session's permissions allowed `uc_solve` but denied other programs:

- `build/uc_verify` checks a solution CSV against the physical rules and recomputes its objective from the schedule.
- `build/uc_unitcheck` compares T with the `base` model, one generator at a time, under random objectives at zero gap. It would catch an invalid inequality far more sensitively than the 0.01% comparison in `RESULTS.md`.
- Scripts in Python and `awk` for the same purposes were also denied, as was a batch script for the runs.

So **both tools compile but have never been executed, and may contain bugs.** No solution's objective has been recomputed by separate code. To run them:

```
build/uc_verify data/NAME.json results/NAME.mip.csv OBJECTIVE
build/uc_unitcheck data/NAME.json
build/uc_unitcheck --variant pw48-printed data/NAME.json
build/uc_unitcheck --variant tail-printed data/NAME.json
```

Because of the same restriction, the data checks that I first wrote as a separate tool became the `data warning` lines in `uc_solve`. A solver should report these anyway, but it is also why they live there.

The paper's Reference implementation (EGRET) and the benchmark library were not consulted, as instructed.

| Historical `w` | `w(1-time_down_t0) = 1` for a unit off at period 0; otherwise 0 | Same reason. It is the only shut-down before the horizon that can pair with a start-up in it. |
| Off-time arcs | `x(t',t)` for `DT <= t-t' <= TC-1`, for `t'` in the horizon or at the historical shut-down. (60) at that shut-down has right side 1. | The nomenclature includes times before the horizon. An off time of n periods at period 0 and a start at t gives an off duration of `t+n-1`, matching "off for at least `lag` periods". |
| Rows at `t = T` | `w(T+1) = 0` in (23), (38), (46), (48) | Section 3 sets `v` and `w` beyond the horizon to 0, so no shut-down limit applies at T. |
| `(38)` and `(40)` for `UT = 1` | Included, with the sum empty or one term | Table 3 has no condition. These rows are dominated by (23) but harmless. |
| `(23)` for `UT > 1` | Not used | The paper defines it for G^1 only. (38) generalizes (20) for the others. |
| Left side of (41) | `p'`, not `p̄'` | It is printed with `p`, and its ramp-down terms do not limit available power. |
| `K^SD(t) <= 0` | (41) omitted | The paper says so. |
| `p'(0)` | `p(0) - P_` if on, else 0 | From (12). |
| Variables | `p`, `p̄`, `c^p`, `c^SU`, `c^SD`, and `s` are not created | (12), (13), (44), (61), (62) and (66) substitute them out, as the paper does for cost variables. `s` is `s+ - s-`. |
| Renewables | One aggregate variable per period, bounds the sum of the unit bounds | (63), for one bus. Only the total is reported. |
| Network | (64) dropped; flow sums in (65) empty | Section 3.9.2, for one bus. |
| `T^RU`, `T^RD` | Floor computed with an added 1e-9 | Protects against rounding in ratios that are exact in the data. |
| Solver settings | Gurobi defaults, 16 threads, except `MIPGap` and `TimeLimit` | Matches the paper's Section 6.3, which keeps defaults apart from the limit and gap. |

## Data preprocessing that is present but not used here

`uc_solve` prints a `data warning` to stderr whenever one of these applies. On the seven instances the only warnings are SU and SD above P̄ (CAISO) and UT and DT above T (FERC), so none of the following is used.

- **Start-up categories:** the paper sets `T^1 = DT`. A first lag above DT is extended down to DT, and categories wholly below DT are dropped.
- **Cost curves:** restricted to `[P_, P̄]` by interpolation, with repeated points removed, so that `P̄^l > P_` and `P̄^0 = P_`. `C^R` is the curve's cost at `P_`.
- **UT, DT below 1:** set to 1.
- **Not repaired, warned only:** decreasing start-up costs, which would break (61); non-convex curves; `p(0)` above `SU + (time_up_t0-1) RU`, which would make the historical `v` terms infeasible; and a must-run unit required to stay off, which is infeasible.

## Output choices the task left open

- `--relax --solution`: `on` is `u` rounded at 0.5, as the format requires 0 or 1. `power` and `available` use the fractional `u`.
- In a MIP solution, `u` is rounded before computing `power` and `available`, which removes integrality noise.
- Besides `objective=` and `bound=`, stdout has `gap=`, `nodes=`, `status=`, `runtime=`, `size=` and totals for slacks and renewables. The Gurobi log is not sent to the console.
- If there is no solution, it prints `objective=nan` and exits 1. An LP stopped by the limit counts as no solution, since its point is not the relaxation's value. A MIP with no finite bound yet prints `bound=-inf`.
- Generator names containing commas or quotes are quoted in the CSV. None of the seven instances has one.

## Options beyond the specified command line

- `--log FILE` keeps the Gurobi log.
- `--variant NAME` selects a diagnostic departure from the default model, and may be repeated. The names are `reserve-printed`, `updown-printed`, `updown-all-periods`, `tail-none`, `tail-printed`, `pw48-printed`, `no-hist-v` and `base`, along with names that restate the defaults. They exist only to measure the decisions above.

## Verification

**What was run.** The checks reported in `RESULTS.md`: T against the `base` model on all seven instances, hand checks of one period and one unit, an independent read-through of the code against the paper, and tests of the early-stop and bad-input paths.

**What could not be run.** This session's permissions allowed `uc_solve` but denied other programs:

- `build/uc_verify` checks a solution CSV against the physical rules and recomputes its objective from the schedule.
- `build/uc_unitcheck` compares T with the `base` model, one generator at a time, under random objectives at zero gap. It would catch an invalid inequality far more sensitively than the 0.01% comparison in `RESULTS.md`.
- Scripts in Python and `awk` for the same purposes were also denied, as was a batch script for the runs.

So **both tools compile but have never been executed, and may contain bugs.** No solution's objective has been recomputed by separate code. To run them:

```
build/uc_verify data/NAME.json results/NAME.mip.csv OBJECTIVE
build/uc_unitcheck data/NAME.json
build/uc_unitcheck --variant pw48-printed data/NAME.json
build/uc_unitcheck --variant tail-printed data/NAME.json
```

Because of the same restriction, the data checks that I first wrote as a separate tool became the `data warning` lines in `uc_solve`. A solver should report these anyway, but it is also why they live there.

The paper's Reference implementation (EGRET) and the benchmark library were not consulted, as instructed.

content.text:
I built `uc_solve` and ran all seven instances: every MIP reached the 0.01% gap in under 60 seconds, and every LP solved to optimality. However, the default model departs from the paper's reserve equation (67), which changes the objective a lot, and no separate code has recomputed the objectives.

| Instance | LP objective | MIP objective | MIP bound | MIP time (s) | MIP objective with (67) as printed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `rts_gmlc_2020-01-27` | 1,226,645.34 | 1,230,475.37 | 1,230,407.98 | 40.8 | 2,895,818.51 |
| `rts_gmlc_2020-07-06` | 3,722,397.47 | 3,729,194.92 | 3,728,825.77 | 4.5 | 4,744,049.17 |
| `rts_gmlc_2020-12-23` | 2,697,031.22 | 2,707,509.12 | 2,707,260.27 | 8.8 | 3,427,596.73 |
| `ca_2014-09-01_reserves_3` | 48,399.53 | 48,409.12 | 48,404.47 | 20.9 | 48,408.25 |
| `ca_Scenario400_reserves_1` | 33,585.58 | 33,590.74 | 33,587.39 | 25.5 | 59,294.77 |
| `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` | 41,480,391.46 | 41,483,157.10 | 41,482,399.55 | 54.5 | 70,853,552.80 |
| `ferc_2015-04-01_lw` | 56,994,290.75 | 57,001,082.95 | 56,999,603.01 | 58.8 | 57,424,327.87 |

## Other departures from the paper
`NOTES.md` has the reasoning and examples for each, plus the smaller choices.
- **Minimum up/down times (4), (5):** FERC units with UT or DT above T get no rows as printed, which lowers the `ferc_2015-01-01_hw` objective by 12.7%. I start those rows at `min(UT,T)` and `min(DT,T)` instead.
- **Printing errors (41), (48):** the K^SU definition refers to itself, and two `[·]^+` terms have their operands reversed, which can cut off feasible schedules. Corrected; the corrections left the LP bound unchanged wherever I measured it.
- **`SU`/`SD` above `Pmax`:** clipped to `Pmax`, which affects 574 of the 610 units in each CAISO instance.

## Verification
- **Blocked:** this session's permissions only allowed `uc_solve` to run, so `uc_verify` (recomputes objectives) and `uc_unitcheck` (tests the inequalities) compile but have never been run and may have bugs. The commands are in `NOTES.md`.
- **Comparison with a basic model:** T agrees with an unstrengthened physical model on all seven instances within the gap, but that can't see errors smaller than about $300 on RTS or $5,000 on FERC. The two models also share the objective, up/down-time and start-up code.
- **Other checks:** one RTS period and one unit's schedule check out by hand, and an independent read of the code against the paper found no defects.

## Decision for you
Should the reserve row keep my added renewable term? As printed, (67) makes thermal capacity alone cover all load, which contradicts the paper's own link between (67) and (68). On `rts_gmlc_2020-01-27` it curtails 61% of free renewable energy instead of 14%. My version also reproduces the paper's ordering of RTS solve times, while the printed form reverses it, though that's only suggestive because the solver and machine differ. To use the literal equation, add `--variant reserve-printed`; the last table column shows the result.

Everything is in `/home/dlw/Documents/Research/uc_rerun/work/`; start with `RESULTS.md` and `NOTES.md`. Solution CSVs and logs are in `results/`.

import json,glob,collections
for f in sorted(glob.glob('data/*.json')):
    d=json.load(open(f))
    print(f, list(d.keys()), 'T',d['time_periods'],'G',len(d['thermal_generators']),'R',len(d['renewable_generators']))
    tg=d['thermal_generators']
    g0=next(iter(tg.values()))
    print(' keys',sorted(g0.keys()))
    print(' dem',min(d['demand']),max(d['demand']),' res',min(d['reserves']),max(d['reserves']))
    stats=collections.Counter()
    for n,g in tg.items():
        Pm,PM=g['power_output_minimum'],g['power_output_maximum']
        SU,SD,RU,RD=g['ramp_startup_limit'],g['ramp_shutdown_limit'],g['ramp_up_limit'],g['ramp_down_limit']
        UT,DT=g['time_up_minimum'],g['time_down_minimum']
        if n!=g['name']: stats['name_mismatch']+=1
        if g['must_run']: stats['must_run']+=1
        if UT==1: stats['UT1']+=1
        if UT==0: stats['UT0']+=1
        if DT==0: stats['DT0']+=1
        if DT==1: stats['DT1']+=1
        if SU<Pm: stats['SU<Pmin']+=1
        if SD<Pm: stats['SD<Pmin']+=1
        if SU>PM: stats['SU>Pmax']+=1
        if SD>PM: stats['SD>Pmax']+=1
        if SU!=SD: stats['SU!=SD']+=1
        if RU<=0 or RD<=0: stats['ramp0']+=1
        if RU>PM-Pm: stats['RU_nonbinding']+=1
        if Pm==PM: stats['Pmin=Pmax']+=1
        if Pm==0: stats['Pmin=0']+=1
        pw=g['piecewise_production']
        if abs(pw[0]['mw']-Pm)>1e-9: stats['pw0!=Pmin']+=1
        if abs(pw[-1]['mw']-PM)>1e-9: stats['pwlast!=Pmax']+=1
        if len(pw)<2: stats['pw<2']+=1
        sl=[(pw[i+1]['cost']-pw[i]['cost'])/(pw[i+1]['mw']-pw[i]['mw']) if pw[i+1]['mw']>pw[i]['mw'] else None for i in range(len(pw)-1)]
        if None in sl: stats['pw_dup_mw']+=1
        elif any(sl[i+1]<sl[i]-1e-9 for i in range(len(sl)-1)): stats['nonconvex']+=1
        su=g['startup']
        if su[0]['lag']!=DT: stats['lag0!=DT']+=1
        stats['startcats=%d'%len(su)]+=1
        if any(su[i+1]['cost']<su[i]['cost'] for i in range(len(su)-1)): stats['su_decreasing']+=1
        if any(su[i+1]['lag']<=su[i]['lag'] for i in range(len(su)-1)): stats['su_lag_nonincr']+=1
        on=g['unit_on_t0']
        if on and g['power_output_t0']<=0: stats['on_p0=0']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']<Pm: stats['on_p0<Pmin']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']>PM: stats['on_p0>Pmax']+=1
        if not on and g['power_output_t0']!=0: stats['off_p0!=0']+=1
        if on and g['time_up_t0']<=0: stats['on_tup0=0']+=1
        if on and g['time_down_t0']!=0: stats['on_tdn!=0']+=1
        if not on and g['time_down_t0']<=0: stats['off_tdn0=0']+=1
        if not on and g['time_up_t0']!=0: stats['off_tup!=0']+=1
        if on and g['power_output_t0']>SD and g['time_up_t0']>=UT and False: pass
        if Pm>SU: stats['Pm>SU']+=1
        for k in g:
            if k not in ('name','startup','piecewise_production') and not isinstance(g[k],(int,float)): stats['type_'+k]+=1
    print(' ',dict(stats))
    rn=d['renewable_generators']
    rm=[sum(r['power_output_minimum'][t] for r in rn.values()) for t in range(d['time_periods'])]
    rM=[sum(r['power_output_maximum'][t] for r in rn.values()) for t in range(d['time_periods'])]
    print(' ren min',max(rm) if rm else None,' max',max(rM) if rM else None)
EOF
